title: Stranded in Chattanooga and the pawned saxophone; leaving Brown in 1927
summary: Hotel owner Mr. Dent feeds the stranded band; they pawn Phil Tiller's sax to reach Sheffield, and in 1927 Pillars leaves Brown to join Brady Bryant's Merrymakers with Louis Jordan.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: We ventured out one year through northern Alabama, up to Chattanooga, Tennessee, and we got stranded in Chattanooga, Tennessee. We were stopping at a hotel called the Dent Hotel. And this is one of the reasons why I love people today, because people have been good to me all my life. When I say me, I mean good to us musicians all of our lives.

We stayed in that hotel. We didn't have money to pay for food -- to pay for food. And Mr. Dent, everytime that dinnertime come, he'd say, 'Come on, boys, and sit at the table. Come on out here and eat.' And he would feed us. And I can remember how we got out of that town. We had two saxophones in the band then. We had a boy named Philander Tiller from Little Rock who I had recommended to join the band. Fernando Tiller had been going to Howard University, and this particular year he had laid out of school.

So, in order to get out of town, Johnny Brown booked our band back to Sheffield, Alabama. And the only way he could do it was to take Phil Tiller's saxophone and ask him would it be all right for us to pawn his horn -- pawn Tiller's horn, and

let Tiller stay there.
And we would go to Sheffield, Alabama where Johnnie Brown had friends, and we had booked ourselves in there for several dances in and around Sheffield. And we pawned the horn for enough money to pay our train fare from there to Sheffield.
As luck would have it,
(Unintelligible) we played a big dance there. We had a big crowd. And Johnnie Brown was able to borrow money from one of the big business people there. He wired the money to Phil Tiller, paid up our bill there, and sent Phil Tiller a ticket to come and join us. And these were the things you had to do back in those days, you know what I mean, when things got rough on you.
Things were really rough back in those days. You didn't make much money, but we all loved each other and we stuck together.
In 1927 I left Johnnie Brown. I went back home. While being back home I started to work with a band named Brady Bryant and his Merrymakers. In that band we had Mr. Brady Bryant -- he played the drums -- and a fellow named George Lot played trumpet. Another fellow named Carl Charleson played trumpet. I played the alto saxophone. And by that time Louis Jordan had left the show, and he was back in Little Rock. So, Louis Jordan and I had a chance to play together in this band.
